items.title: Chick Corea — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I recorded the Tadd Dameron tune, “Hot House,” with Gary Burton recently... I’ve also been on tour with Gary Burton and a string quartet... Manfred Eicher became a help to the duet because he was the first one who suggested that we do a recording, which resulted in our first record, Crystal Silence.

ctx.x: I gather with Pete Yellin you had a rehearsal band (speaking of drummer-priests) in which Milford Graves was playing timbales, and you were playing bebop tunes and doing what they now call ‘the Latin Side of’ or something...

That was a fun band. And I’ve got to connect up with Milford again. It’s been too many years. I know he’s active in doing a lot or creative stuff. But the spirit of that band... That was Pete Yellin, Lisle Atkinson was the bass player, Milford and myself. I think Bill Fitch played some conga in that band. The idea was me and Pete wanted to take all of the Charlie Parker tunes that we loved and put them into a salsa beat, into a mambo beat. In fact, remembering those days... items.doc: Gary Burton NEA Jazz Master Oral History Interview-1
items.title: Gary Burton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: We tour every year. We’ve put out I think eight records together, and we’ve won five Grammys so far for those records.

ctx.x: Ok. I saw you two or three weeks ago. You had just been honored NEA Jazz Master. What was that feeling... Tell me your reaction when you first learned you became an NEA Jazz Master.

Well, it was not a total surprise, because I’ve watched quite a few of my friends and co-performers, collaborators—Carla Bley, Chick Corea, Keith Jarrett and so on—be given this honor in recent years. So I’ve said to myself, “Well, there’s probably a chance that I might get called one of these days.” So it didn’t totally come out of the blue, but nonetheless felt great to hear that I had been chosen for my career, for my life, to be honored in this way.
